explanation: AB = √3, BC = √3 and AC = 2√3 = AB + BC, so B lies on AC.

text: A general point on the z-axis has coordinates:
explanation: On the z-axis both x and y are zero.

text: The point on the x-axis equidistant from (1, 2, 3) and (3, 5, −2) is:
The triangle with vertices (0, 7, −10), (1, 6, −6) and (4, 9, −6) is:
explanation: AB = BC = √18 and AC = 6; AB² + BC² = 36 = AC², so it is right-angled at B and isosceles.

text: The three coordinate planes divide space into how many octants?
explanation: Each of x, y, z can be positive or negative: 2³ = 8 octants.

text: The distance of the point (4, −3, 5) from the xy-plane is:
explanation: Distance from the xy-plane is |z| = 5.

text: If the origin is the centroid of the triangle with vertices (2a, 2, 6), (−4, 3b, −10) and (8, 14, 2c), then (a, b, c) is:
explanation: Each coordinate sum must be 0: 2a − 4 + 8 = 0 ⇒ a = −2; 2 + 3b + 14 = 0 ⇒ b = −16/3; 6 − 10 + 2c = 0 ⇒ c = 2.

text: The set of points P(x, y, z) equidistant from A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, 2, −1) satisfies:
explanation: PA² = PB² ⇒ (x − 1)² + (z − 3)² = (x − 3)² + (z + 1)² (the y-terms cancel) ⇒ 4x − 8z = 0 ⇒ x − 2z = 0.

text: Which of the following is a statement (in the logical sense)?
explanation: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false, not both. '2 + 3 = 6' is a false statement; commands, exclamations and open sentences are not statements.

text: The negation of '√2 is irrational' is:
explanation: Negation simply reverses the truth: 'It is not the case that √2 is irrational', i.e. √2 is rational.

text: The negation of 'All birds can fly' is:
options: There exists a bird that cannot fly
explanation: The negation of 'for all' is 'there exists … not'. 'No bird can fly' is far stronger than what is needed.

text: The negation of p ∧ q is:
explanation: De Morgan's law for statements: ∼(p ∧ q) ≡ ∼p ∨ ∼q.

text: The contrapositive of 'If a number is divisible by 9, then it is divisible by 3' is:
options: If a number is not divisible by 3, then it is not divisible by 9
A number is divisible by 9 and not by 3
If a number is divisible by 3, then it is divisible by 9
If a number is not divisible by 9, then it is not divisible by 3
explanation: The contrapositive of p ⇒ q is ∼q ⇒ ∼p. Option 2 is the converse and option 3 the inverse.

text: The converse of 'If a number is divisible by 9, then it is divisible by 3' is:
options: If a number is not divisible by 9, then it is not divisible by 3
If a number is not divisible by 3, then it is not divisible by 9
If a number is divisible by 3, then it is divisible by 9
A number is divisible by 9 if and only if it is divisible by 3
explanation: The converse of p ⇒ q is q ⇒ p. (Here the converse is false: 6 is divisible by 3 but not by 9.)

text: The compound statement p ∨ q is false only when:
options: both p and q are false
p is false and q is true
both p and q are true
p is true and q is false
explanation: An inclusive 'or' is true if at least one component is true.

text: The compound statement p ∧ q is true only when:
options: exactly one of p, q is true
at least one of p, q is true
both p and q are false
both p and q are true
explanation: 'And' requires every component to be true.

text: The implication p ⇒ q is false only when:
options: p is true and q is false
p is false and q is true
explanation: A promise 'if p then q' is broken only when p happens and q does not.

text: The statement p ⇒ q is logically equivalent to:
explanation: A statement and its contrapositive always have the same truth value; the converse and inverse need not.

text: The truth value of 'There exists a real number x such that x² < 0' is:
explanation: For every real x, x² ≥ 0, so no such x exists.

text: The negation of 'For every real number x, x² ≥ 0' is:
options: There exists a real number x such that x² ≥ 0
For every real number x, x² < 0
There exists a real number x such that x² < 0
For every real number x, x² ≤ 0
explanation: ∼(∀x, P(x)) ≡ ∃x, ∼P(x), and the negation of x² ≥ 0 is x² < 0.

text: The biconditional p ⇔ q is true exactly when:
options: p and q have different truth values
p and q have the same truth value
explanation: p ⇔ q means (p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p); it holds when both are true or both are false.

text: To prove 'If n² is even, then n is even' (n an integer), the most convenient method is to prove:
options: If n is even, then n² is even
If n² is odd, then n is odd
n² is even for every n
If n is odd, then n² is odd
explanation: That is the contrapositive (∼q ⇒ ∼p): n = 2m + 1 gives n² = 2(2m² + 2m) + 1, odd. Option 2 is the converse, which does not prove the claim.

text: The compound statement '7 is a prime number or 7 is even' is:
options: true, since the first component is true
true, since both components are true
explanation: For 'or', one true component is enough.

text: A counter-example to the statement 'If n is a prime number, then n is odd' is:
explanation: 2 is prime but even, so the hypothesis holds while the conclusion fails. 9 is odd but not prime — not a counter-example to this statement.

text: The negation of 'x > 3 or x < 1' is:
explanation: ∼(p ∨ q) ≡ ∼p ∧ ∼q; the negation of x > 3 is x ≤ 3 and of x < 1 is x ≥ 1.

text: The number of rows in the truth table of a compound statement built from 3 simple statements is:
explanation: Each statement is T or F: 2³ = 8 combinations.
